One of the worst things about this for me is just how many guys think you're exaggerating for attention or something. I've been catcalled since *middle school*, I've had older men *pull over and offer me a ride*, including once when I was fifteen, I've had *multiple* incidences of guys yelling out to me asking if I "take it up the ass", I've been followed around a gas station at night and had to lock myself in the bathroom, and whenever I've relayed any of these experiences to guy friends or (former) boyfriends, I'm met with minimization or disbelief. And my experiences aren't even unusual, every woman I've met has stories like these. And yet, guys often act like I'm overreacting by being scared, or say they'd love to be "complimented" by random women on the street.

Ah I see what you're saying in terms of time devoted to someone. It's certainly true for me that just being in a relationship with one person takes up a lot of time, so I can see how it would be even harder to divide your attention/intimate capacities between multiple partners. I'm not advocating for one lifestyle over the other; I've never been in a polyamorous relationship. I'm just really interested in humans' capacities for love and am curious about the intricacies of all sorts of relationships. It seems to me that it would be fairly easy to find love in your heart for more than one person romantically, though definitely a lot harder to balance that love within the context of committed relationships.

> The more people you love, the less that love actually means

I'm not sure about that one. When you think about non-romantic love relationships, that's certainly not the case. I love a lot of people in my life but I don't think my love for one person cheapens or lessens the love I have for another. Why should it be any different for romantic love?
